newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia pays army back wages as taxes flow in - aide.
newsitem.headline: Russia pays army back wages as taxes flow in - aide.

text.p: Finance Minister Alexander Livshits has said Russia, preparing to tap world markets with a debut Eurobond this month, was paying wage arrears to the military after an improvement in tax collection.

Servicemen are caught in Russia's payments crisis, in which millions of workers have gone unpaid for months. Defence Minister Igor Rodionov warned last month that the cash-strapped forces were on the brink of "uncontrollable developments".
But Livshits told radio station Ekho Moskvy at the weekend that tax revenues had picked up last month and military wage arrears were being cleared.
"Everything due for October is being handed over, plus a small amount due for July that still remains. Everything due for November is being handed over, plus some of what's due for August," he said.

The International Monetary Fund, worried about low tax collection, last month delayed payment of a tranche of a $10 billion loan to Russia. An IMF mission is to return to Moscow later this week for more talks.
The government has stepped up efforts in collecting taxes by setting up an emergency committee with wide punitive powers and threatening some corporate tax-dodgers with bankruptcy proceedings.
"Tax revenues have improved in October after the government exerted pressure on most bad non-payers," Finance Ministry Macroeconomy Department Head Pavel Zhukov told Reuters.
Official figures for late September showed workers were owed more than 40 trillion roubles ($7.3 billion) by the government and companies.
Zhukov said October tax revenue rose to 22 trillion roubles from 17 trillion in September, according to early data.
But Livshits said that despite the improvement, Russia could not be sure of receiving the IMF money.
"The (November) talks will be difficult," he said.
Russia has mainly covered its budget gap by issuing domestic securities, but has plans to tap international markets as well.
Its 1997 draft budget provides for foreign borrowing, mainly from international commercial banks and firms, of 7.24 trillion roubles compared with 1.65 trillion this year.
Livshits said Russia would issue its first Eurobond between November 21 and 25.
"We want to place our paper at comparatively low price. The first issue will be around $500 million. It may be less."
Russia received better-than-expected credit ratings from the world's leading ratings agencies, paving the way for its first sovereign bond since the 1917 Bolshevik Revolution.
Lead managers JP Morgan and SBC Warburg are due to begin a series of presentations to investors on the issue on Monday.
Back in tsarist days, Russia issued bonds to pay for railroad construction and other projects.
But after the Bolsheviks came to power, they refused to pay back the bonds, leaving millions of investors holding beautiful, but virtually worthless paper.

Last month Livshits said Russia was close to a deal to pay the tsarist-era debts. It has already reached rescheduling deals with the London Club of commercial banks and Paris Club of government creditors.
"We want to be there (on the Western markets) not for some time, but forever. They trust us and we want to look good."
